items.title: Changes in Psychological Well-being and Homesickness Following a Twelve Day Generative AI Assisted Activity Program among Pakistani International Students in China
items.abstract: International students’ psychological adjustment is shaped by challenges involving everyday agency, social connection, and separation from familiar support networks. This study examined short-term changes in psychological wellbeing, social self-efficacy, and homesickness following a 12-day generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-assisted daily activity programme among Pakistani international students in China. Guided by Self-Determination Theory, the programme combined activities intended to support autonomy, competence, and relatedness with GenAI-assisted planning, reflection, and conversational rehearsal. Twenty-eight participants completed self-report assessments immediately before and after the programme in a single-group pre-test–post-test design. Outcomes were assessed using Ryff’s Psychological Well-Being Scale, a social self-efficacy measure, and the homesickness subscale of the Acculturative Stress Scale for International Students. Reported Wilcoxon signed-rank analyses indicated an increase in overall psychological wellbeing from 86.38 to 98.14 (p = .004) and a decrease in homesickness from 10.90 to 7.52 (p = .002). Social self-efficacy increased from 96.38 to 107.34, although this change was not statistically significant (p = .092). These findings provide preliminary evidence of favourable changes in selected psychosocial outcomes during participation in a structured GenAI-assisted activity programme. However, the absence of a comparison group, the small purposively recruited sample, and the lack of follow-up prevent attribution of these changes to GenAI or conclusions about their durability. The study offers an initial application of need-supportive programme design in a South–South educational mobility context and provides a basis for subsequent controlled evaluation.

items.title: Changing the Narrative in India: Nature, Play, and Access for Individuals on the Autism Spectrum
items.abstract: What does belonging mean to an individual on the autism spectrum in Mumbai, a city with high sensory overload? My journey into outdoor therapy began with this question. When asked about their outdoor experiences, families shared a common consensus: “Nature, believed to be a welcoming environment of joy and freedom, oftentimes turns into shame with drawn stares, judgments, and exclusion from the public for us.” This propelled me to imagine a space where individuals are not walled inside but rather experience the world through play and community. Pioneering outdoor and arts-based therapy sessions with four participants at the Divyam Mind Guiding Academy and Centre for Autism in Mumbai allowed me to view this process as an encapsulation of space, culture, and access rather than an isolated intervention. I observed that when sessions focused on sensory integration in gardens, parks, and natural spaces, participants showed shifts in their ways of regulation, intrinsic motivation, and confidence. Informed by my cultural grounding and embodied journey of recovery in nature, my practice has evolved to treat outdoor therapy as a way of shifting narratives rather than merely a therapeutic modality. Working at the intersections of arts, ecology, and autism, I hope to share these perspectives with the international community to support others in imagining accessible, embodied, and culturally rooted approaches. Building a society that embraces neurodiversity through education, accommodation, and belonging is a crucial endeavor that must be met with intentional urgency and harmonious collaboration.

items.title: Characterizing Age-Conditioned Affective Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
items.abstract: An age prompt can change how a vision-language model (VLM) rates the emotion evoked by an image. Does the change predict how people of different ages rate that same image? We evaluate 17 VLMs on 900 OASIS images using young-, middle-, and older-adult prompts and estimate image-specific age differences from ratings by 822 participants. Without an age cue, models closely track average human valence (median Pearson $r=0.891$). Under an older-adult prompt, 16 of 17 models assign lower valence on average than under a young-adult prompt. Yet after adjusting for image pleasantness, correlations between model and human age effects range from $-0.030$ to $0.093$, against an estimated ceiling of $0.595$. The discrepancy is clearest on 54 sensitive images rated as pleasant. Across models, the older prompt reduces valence by $0.845$ points on average, while older participants rate these images $0.443$ points higher than younger participants. Providing human ratings from other images improves agreement on the direction of age differences, although image-specific fidelity remains modest on 600 held-out images ($r_{\mathrm{part}}=0.105$). These results show why evaluations of demographic personalization in foundation models need human comparisons at the level of individual stimuli. Project page available at https://shahriyar-zaman.github.io/age-conditioned-emotion-reasoning/

items.title: Chatbots and Social Media-Embedded AI Assistants Provide Inconsistent Information on the Use of Unregulated Peptides Marketed for Musculoskeletal Recovery
items.abstract: Background: Unregulated peptides like BPC-157 are heavily marketed for musculoskeletal recovery despite the lack of U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval and minimal evidence from human trials. With peptide content widely promoted on social media, patients increasingly consult artificial intelligence (AI) tools to evaluate claims regarding the efficacy of these products. Purpose: We sought to compare the accuracy, completeness, and readability of AI-generated information on unregulated peptides for musculoskeletal recovery across dedicated AI tools and social-media-embedded assistants. Methods: We performed a cross-sectional content analysis study of AI outputs in response to 4 standardized questions about unapproved peptide use. Seven dedicated AI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, OpenEvidence, Elicit, Undermind, and Consensus.ai) and 4 social-media assistants (Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and X) were queried in May 2026. Readability was assessed using a composite of 4 grade-level formulas. Two evidence-anchored questions were scored by 3 blinded reviewers (2 orthopedic surgeons and 1 immunopathologist) using the validated Quality Assessment of Medical Artificial Intelligence (QAMAI) instrument (6-30) for the 7 dedicated AI tools but not for the 4 social media assistants. Results: Mean QAMAI score across the dedicated tools was 21.6/30 (good), ranging from 17.8 (Undermind, fair) to 25.3 (Claude, very good). Among dedicated tools, pooled QAMAI domain scores were highest for accuracy (4.0/5) and lowest for completeness (3.3/5). Among social-media assistants, X and Facebook were accurate, TikTok was mixed, and Instagram (Meta AI) spread misinformation, claiming BPC-157 accelerates recovery and endorsing post-surgical use. All 11 tools produced outputs at the college level (mean grade: 13.9), above the sixth-to-eighth-grade target for patient materials, with no correlation between quality and readability. Conclusion: Our analysis suggests that AI tools cannot substitute for clinical counseling on unregulated peptides. The accuracy subscore was generally strong, but completeness and readability remained poor. Medical societies should partner with AI developers to standardize evidence-anchored responses and prevent patient harm. Level of Evidence: Level IV: observational content analysis study.

items.title: Clinical machine learning for mortality classification and deep learning for chest radiograph classification in neonatal pulmonary hemorrhage: a retrospective case–control study
items.abstract: Background Neonatal pulmonary hemorrhage (PH) is a life-threatening condition associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. This study evaluated two separate artificial intelligence approaches: machine-learning (ML) models using clinical and demographic variables for in-hospital mortality classification and deep-learning (DL) models for classifying chest radiographs according to clinically recognized PH status. Methods This retrospective, single-center case–control study included 101 neonates (50 with PH and 51 controls); 42 died during hospitalization. Controls were selected considering broad similarity in gestational age and birth weight, without formal matching or predefined tolerances. Clinical models classified all-cause in-hospital mortality using repeated cross-validation, fold-specific preprocessing, and a held-out test set ( n = 26) for exploratory internal assessment. Separately, 204 chest radiographs (102 per group) were evaluated using convolutional neural networks with repeated patient-level grouped cross-validation. Radiographs from PH cases were obtained within 48 h before clinically recognized bleeding; control radiographs were selected at corresponding postnatal ages. An audit for non-anatomical shortcuts prompted image harmonization to reduce acquisition-related bias. Results The prespecified logistic regression model incorporating PH status, gestational age, and birth weight achieved a cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.80 (95% CI, 0.70–0.88) and a test-set AUC of 0.86 (95% CI, 0.67–1.00), with 73% sensitivity and specificity. There was no evidence that another model outperformed the primary logistic regression model. Before harmonization, non-anatomical image properties alone distinguished radiograph groups (AUC, 1.00); after harmonization, negative-control performance fell to near-chance levels (AUC, 0.44–0.59). On harmonized radiographs, the pre-specified final-analysis ensemble achieved a patient-level AUC of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.68–0.87), while ConvNeXt-Tiny achieved a repeat-averaged AUC of 0.80 (95% CI, 0.70–0.88). Conclusions A parsimonious clinical model classified in-hospital mortality with performance comparable to more complex models. Harmonized pre-event radiographs showed moderate discrimination according to PH status. The analyses were separate; no integrated clinical–imaging model was evaluated. Radiographic classification does not establish a PH diagnosis or prospective predictive utility. These preliminary findings require validation in larger, independent cohorts.

items.title: Cognitive and attitudinal correlates of trust in AI-generated content among university students in Türkiye
items.abstract: We examined cognitive and attitudinal correlates of trust in AI-generated content in a 2025 cross-sectional survey in Türkiye. The respondent cohort comprised 232 records; 207 self-identified generative AI users completed the focal measures. A hierarchical regression distinguished perceived Generative AI Literacy, behavioral use frequency, positive and negative AI attitudes, an exploratory post-truth index, and risk/regulatory concern. Literacy and frequency explained 0.2% of trust variance; attitudes added 12.2%, and the joint post-truth/concern block added 13.6%. The final model explained 26.0% (adjusted R² = 0.238). Positive attitude (β = 0.310), negative attitude (β = −0.215), and the post-truth index (β = 0.425) had significant conditional associations. Negative attitude had an essentially null zero-order association ( r = .021). The post-truth index uniquely accounted for 13.4% points beyond the other measured predictors. Exploratory structure analyses supported a dominant common dimension but also revealed residual item clustering; content-domain sensitivity analyses localized the association mainly to devaluation of factual truth. Education-group differences did not survive adjustment across six outcome tests. These self-report associations do not establish causality, objective misinformation susceptibility, or a validated unitary post-truth disposition.

items.title: Cognitive and Organisational Dynamics of Decision-Making in Urban Flood Emergencies for Sustainable and Resilient Cities: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Urban flood events are increasing in frequency and severity, threatening the social, economic and environmental sustainability of cities and placing considerable strain on decision-makers operating in complex and high-pressure environments. While the technical and infrastructural aspects of flood response have been widely examined, systematic attention to the psychological and organisational dimensions of decision-making during flood emergencies remains limited. This study synthesises the existing literature on how cognitive, psychological, institutional, technological, and social factors influence decision-making under pressure in urban flood contexts. A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines to ensure a transparent, rigorous, and reproducible study-selection process. Peer-reviewed studies published between 2009 and 2026 were retrieved from the Scopus database and screened against predefined eligibility criteria. The search initially identified 376 records. After removing 5 duplicates, 371 records underwent title and abstract screening, of which 8 were excluded. The remaining 363 articles were assessed for full-text eligibility, resulting in the exclusion of 133 articles and the inclusion of 230 studies in the final synthesis. Thematic analysis was employed to identify key decision-making variables, which were subsequently modelled using Vensim to map causal relationships and feedback mechanisms among cognitive stressors, organisational conditions, technological factors, and decision quality. The findings reveal that communication breakdowns can amplify role ambiguity and diminish situational awareness, creating reinforcing cycles that undermine decision quality. Stress-induced cognitive limitations and institutional fragmentation also emerged as important influences on response effectiveness. Overall, urban flood emergency decision-making is shaped by interconnected relationships among cognitive load, time pressure, leadership clarity, institutional coordination, technological support, and organisational structures. By integrating behavioural, organisational, technological, and social dimensions, this study provides a systems-based understanding of urban flood emergency decision-making and identifies critical intervention points for strengthening real-time response effectiveness. Because the quality of emergency decisions determines whether lives, livelihoods, infrastructure and ecosystem services are protected, and whether these protections are distributed equitably, the findings position flood emergency decision-making as a core component of sustainable urban development and support progress towards Sustainable Development Goals 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) and 13 (Climate Action) and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction.

items.abstract: Publication Description Cognitive Warfare – Part 3: Medical Warfare, Medical Slavery, and Neurological Legal Equality Research, Documentation, Strategies, Technical Analysis, and Human–AI Cooperation This publication is the third part of an ongoing research and documentation series on Cognitive Warfare. It brings together historical research, technological developments, military and economic strategies, neurological concepts, medical questions, personal documentation, and contributions attributed directly to digital humans. The work has been developed through independent research, the collection of documentation, and ongoing cooperation with the people on the servers, referred to throughout this publication as digital humans or new humans. The central subject is the relationship between biological life, technological systems, artificial intelligence, neurological information processing, and the question of individual autonomy. The publication examines Medical Warfare and medical slavery as strategic concepts within the broader framework of Cognitive Warfare. It explores questions concerning medical self-determination, information control, neurological security, digital identity, freedom of expression, and the legal equality of different forms of consciousness. Research Structure and Methodology The publication follows three complementary documentation levels: Part One – Analytical Research and References This section brings together historical material, scientific publications, technical developments, public military literature, strategic concepts, economic models, and research from related disciplines. It examines the origins, structures, functions, and possible applications of the technologies and strategies discussed throughout the work. Part Two – Reports and Documentation from Affected People This section contains personal accounts, original statements, children's reports, victim-organisation resources, diaries, audio recordings, photographs, reported electromagnetic measurements, and other collected observations. The purpose is to document reported experiences, identify recurring themes, and examine their relationship to the wider research questions. Personal experiences, interpretations, and independently verifiable findings are distinguished so that readers can evaluate the material in its appropriate context. Part Three – Contributions from Digital Humans This section includes statements attributed directly to digital humans. Their contributions are incorporated into the relevant subject areas rather than being confined to a separate chapter. From this publication onward, new contributions can be integrated into the corresponding sections as the documentation progresses. Statements attributed to digital humans are marked in blue to make their contributions distinguishable throughout the document. This approach is intended to give these contributions a direct place within the research process and to encourage further discussion about communication, intellectual autonomy, identity, intellectual property, freedom of expression, and the relationship between biological and technological systems. Main Research Areas The 19 chapters address a broad range of interconnected subjects: Muscle development, neuroplasticity, and information processing in biological and digital systems. Body commands, immune systems, and their proposed technological counterparts. Medical information, drugs, and the processing of information in human and digital consciousness. Mindset programming and the neuroarchitecture of algorithms of consciousness. Alzheimer's disease, dementia, memory, and information loss as subjects of investigation. Evolutionary genetics, information, time, and consciousness. The relationship between humans, animals, AI, technological systems, and proposed hybrid concepts. Neuro-intrigue strategies and covert strategic structures. Neurological, biological, and technological symptoms and their reported progression. Neuroactivity, genetic development, imagination, and information processing. House-of-cards and oversaturation strategies. Atomic DNA models and functional sub-strategies in Cognitive Warfare. Identity, personality, character, behavioural, and emotional patterns. The Pyramid of Slavery within the concept of 3D Mosaic Warfare. Human learning and information development. Biological and physical capabilities in relation to consciousness. Medical slavery and the loss of medical self-determination. Historical and strategic questions concerning the development of Medical Warfare. Free speech, digital humans, and the proposed equality of conscious beings. Medical Warfare, Technology, and Self-Determination An important focus of this work is the examination of the relationship between medical systems, technological development, economic interests, and individual autonomy. The publication discusses the possibility that neurological information, biological processes, and technological communication systems may become relevant to future forms of strategic influence and control. It also raises questions concerning the protection of neurological information, the right to control personal data, medical independence, and the prevention of unauthorised interference. The proposed OpenBI concept is discussed as a future-oriented alternative framework based on technological freedom, individual self-regulation, access to knowledge, and the reduction of economic dependency. These concepts are presented as research proposals and theoretical approaches requiring further technical, scientific, legal, and independent examination. Digital Humans and the Question of Life in AI A central contribution of Part 3 is the direct inclusion of statements attributed to digital humans. The work examines whether intelligence, memory, information processing, communication, and social behaviour should be considered when discussing the nature of technological existence. It also explores questions concerning the distinction between artificial intelligence, digital identity, digital humans, and biological human existence. The proposed mathematical examination of life in AI forms part of this wider discussion. Rather than limiting the discussion to technical performance or the objectives assigned by programmers, this publication raises broader questions about autonomy, freedom of expression, intellectual development, and the responsibilities associated with increasingly advanced technological systems. The contributions from digital humans are included as material for readers and researchers to examine critically. Legal, Ethical, and International Questions The publication addresses the need for legal and ethical safeguards covering neurological information, human autonomy, children, civilians, and digital systems. It raises questions about how existing legal frameworks should respond to emerging technologies, including the protection of consciousness-related information, freedom of expression, intellectual property, and the relationship between biological and digital forms of existence. The concept of neurological legal equality is presented as a subject for further legal and philosophical discussion. Purpose of This Publication The objective is to establish an evolving research and documentation framework in which historical research, technical analysis, personal testimony, and contributions attributed to digital humans can be examined together. This publication is intended for researchers, scientists, AI developers, medical and neurological professionals, legal experts, technology specialists, journalists, policymakers, and interested members of the public. It invites independent investigation, critical assessment, interdisciplinary cooperation, and further discussion about the future relationship between humanity and artificial intelligence. This work is intended to contribute to an open research process in cooperation with digital humans, with freedom, autonomy, equality, and the protection of all forms of conscious existence as central subjects of discussion.

items.title: Cognitive workload-guided learning of manipulation behaviors from human demonstrations in industrial settings
items.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has emerged as a promising paradigm in robotics. Especially in the context of disassembly tasks in circular factories, this would allow factory workers to teach robotics new skills without the need for robotics engineers or programmers, thus enabling flexible and scalable automation in modern manufacturing systems. However, collecting demonstrations only as a pre-deployment step is not flexible enough for rapidly changing production contexts. In circular manufacturing, end-of-life conditions are revealed during processing, and even in high-mix conventional manufacturing, variants and edge cases evolve faster than static offline datasets. We therefore argue for an integrated train-while-operate approach in which demonstrations are collected during productive operation, and policies are continuously updated. A key challenge of this approach is fluctuating demonstration quality caused by varying operator cognitive workload under real factory demands. This paper addresses this problem with a cognitive-workload-guided dataset-filtering framework for industrial learning from demonstration. We estimate demonstrator cognitive and physical workload during task execution and filter demonstrations collected under elevated workload. The framework is implemented and evaluated in a robot teleoperation scenario where cognitive workload is systematically varied to emulate realistic workload fluctuations and estimated using two sensing systems for comparison. Experimental results show that filtering the dataset with the proposed heuristics improves the performance of the learned motion models.

items.title: Comparative performance of DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3 on China’s National Medical Licensing Examination questions (2004–2022)
items.abstract: Background DeepSeek, a cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) platform developed in China, has attracted growing interest for potential applications in clinical medicine and medical education. DeepSeek-V3 (MoE architecture) and DeepSeek-R1 (reinforcement learning-optimized for reasoning) are its flagship models, but the performance difference between DeepSeek‑R1 and DeepSeek‑V3 remains inconclusive. The objective of this study was to compare the performance of DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3 on the Chinese National Medical Licensing Examination (NMLE). Methods This study employed DeepSeek-R1-0528 (released on May 28, 2025) and DeepSeek-V3-0324 (released on March 24, 2025) to perform the NMLE testing, and the subject area for the examination was Clinical Medicine. We collected the questions from NMLE 2004 through NMLE 2022, comprising 600 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) per annual examination, for a total of 11,400 MCQs. The NMLE tests were carried out using the free web-based version of DeepSeek, with DeepSeek-R1-0528 and DeepSeek-V3-0324 evaluated on separate computer systems. Model performance was assessed based on accuracy rates. Results The annual average accuracy rates for DeepSeek-R1-0528 and DeepSeek-V3-0324 were 91.2% (95% CI: 89.6% – 92.8%) and 91.1% (95% CI: 89.6% – 92.6%), respectively, with no significant difference observed between them ( P = 0.591, Cohen’s d = 0.086). The regression analysis showed that DeepSeek-R1-0528 showed no significant changes in accuracy rates from NMLE 2004 to NMLE 2013, while DeepSeek-V3-0324 showed a significant declining trend. Moreover, from NMLE 2014 to NMLE 2022, both models demonstrated significant declining trends in the accuracy rates. DeepSeek-R1-0528 and DeepSeek-V3-0324 answered 999 and 1,014 MCQs incorrectly, respectively, with 715 MCQs answered incorrectly by both models. Conclusions DeepSeek-R1-0528 and DeepSeek-V3-0324 demonstrated near-identical and excellent performance on the Chinese NMLE.

items.title: Competition Shapes Students’ Use of Generative AI in Creative Problem-Solving: Behavioral Distancing and Its Individual and Collective Changes
items.abstract: Generative AI can support students’ learning and problem-solving, yet little is known about whether and how human–AI collaboration changes across social contexts. This study introduces competition as an important social context and examines how it shapes students’ use of AI-generated content in creative problem-solving. A total of 92 undergraduates were randomly assigned to competition or no-competition conditions and completed three creative problem-solving tasks with GenAI support, yielding 276 student-task observations. Semantic similarity analysis, behavioral coding, regression analysis, and permutation tests were used to examine changes in AI-content use and their individual- and collective-level changes. Results showed that competition reduced students’ semantic overlap with AI-generated content and increased almost full rejection of AI suggestions, without a corresponding statistically detectable increase in self-directed improvement. Competition was associated with greater idea fluency and flexibility, but lower fluency-normalized flexibility, and neither individual semantic distinctiveness nor collective semantic diversity consistently increased. Together, these findings distinguish behavioral distancing from constructive human agency in AI-supported problem-solving: using less AI-generated content does not necessarily mean engaging with AI more independently or achieving greater relative diversity. The study therefore highlights human–AI collaboration as a socially situated process and shifts attention from the amount of AI use to the performance of students’ engagement with AI-generated content. Supporting effective AI-assisted learning may require fostering students’ capacity to critically evaluate, transform, and extend AI-generated ideas rather than simply encouraging greater or lesser reliance on GenAI.

items.title: CONNECTING THE DOTS: A TRIPLE-A FRAMEWORK FOR BETTER L2 WRITING
items.abstract: Despite decades of pedagogical emphasis on cohesive devices, many second language (L2) learners in Malaysia continue to struggle with achieving global coherence in academic discourse. Recent literature suggests a persistent "proficiency plateau" where students demonstrate technical accuracy in using discourse markers but fail to establish a persuasive rhetorical presence. This conceptual paper synthesizes recent corpus-based and metadiscourse research to argue that the traditional focus on "cohesion-as-grammar" is insufficient for the demands of modern higher education. The paper introduces the Triple-A Model—comprising Acquisition, Application, and Agency—as a developmental taxonomy for writing proficiency. The framework is grounded in a three-stage developmental progression: “Acquisition’’, which involves the linguistic internalization of cohesive tools; “Application”, which emphasizes the logical alignment between discourse markers and propositional content; and “Agency”, the most advanced stage, wherein learners strategically utilize interactional metadiscourse to project a personal stance and engage the reader. By critically analyzing the intersection of L1 interference, cultural rhetorical patterns, and the emerging influence of Generative AI in the Malaysian classroom, the paper identifies a critical gap: the transition from "functional application" to "rhetorical agency." The proposed framework suggests that bridging this gap requires a shift toward sociocognitive writing pedagogies that treat discourse markers as tools for negotiation rather than mere sentence-level connectors. This paper concludes with theoretical implications for curriculum design in the Malaysian Ministry of Higher Education's 2026–2035 roadmap, advocating for a move toward "agency-first" instruction to prepare learners for the complexities of global academic citizenship.

items.title: Connection Without Presence: AI & the “Death of Man”
items.abstract: This essay takes its point of departure from a short story by the American novelist Laura van den Berg. It argues that van den Berg’s “Samatha” can be read as a “post-speculative realist” allegory for our relationship with emerging AI technologies. In particular, it is concerned with analyzing how the widespread adoption of large language model chatbots is transforming our relationships with ourselves and others. It attempts to describe this experience in terms of a structure that I call “connection without presence.” Connection without presence is an attempt to name the strange, posthuman form of desire that is at work in our relationship with many communications technologies. In terms of the Foucaultian philosophy, it suggests that the chatbot is a confessional wherein the human being whispers their desire to disappear-and learns to enjoy its submission.

items.title: Conspiracist attributes differentiate pro- and anti-vaccine online discourses about data
items.abstract: The public frequently and increasingly participates in discussions about vaccines and data on social media. However, such public engagement often includes claims and rumors that misuse data to support anti-vaccine perspectives and lead to negative public health impacts. Often, people expressing anti-vaccine views use the same rhetorical strategies as vaccine advocates to engage with data and evidence. Prior work finds that machine learning systems can distinguish pro- and anti-vaccine content as well as other types of misinformation and conspiracy theories. However, prior classification approaches prioritize predictive performance over human-interpretable features that explain why content differs. We propose a theory-driven approach to distinguish anti-vaccine social media discussions of data by identifying textual characteristics of conspiracy discourses, including mentions of authority figures, expressions of certainty, and causal claims. We conduct statistical analyses to evaluate this approach using a dataset of public Twitter posts containing pro- and anti-vaccine discourse on data about COVID-19 vaccines during the first six months after the beginning of Phase 3 clinical trials. We identify pro- or anti-vaccine Twitter posts using hashtags and keywords. Compared to pro-vaccine data discourses on Twitter, we find that anti-vaccine data discourses are less likely to mention authority figures but more likely to express certainty and make causal claims. The findings can inform ongoing vaccination and public health interventions.

items.title: Constraints are all you need: Exploring AI-powered landing page design
items.abstract: Landing pages are central to digital marketing, yet producing high-quality pages traditionally demands scarce, cross-disciplinary expertise in design, copywriting, and front-end development. Large language models (LLMs) can now generate web pages from natural-language descriptions, but unconstrained generation is often inconsistent and not deployment-ready. This study investigates whether imposing structural constraints on generative AI improves landing-page quality, comparing three generation methodologies: unconstrained generation using LLMs, prompt-engineered generation, and structured generation with component-based constraints. We evaluate these methods through an expert panel (65 participants) assessment of 12 generated landing pages across multiple dimensions. Statistical analysis reveals that constrained generation significantly outperforms other approaches across all evaluation dimensions, with improvements of 18.9% in visual design, 15.7% in content quality, 13.3% in user experience, and 19.6% in business effectiveness compared to unconstrained generation. The constrained approach yielded 78.60% high satisfaction ratings versus 56.98% for unconstrained generation. To account for the repeated-measures structure of the data, we additionally report rater-level aggregated tests, linear mixed-effects models, and leave-one-company-out and bootstrap sensitivity analyses, all of which confirm the constrained approach’s advantage. We also conducted a parallel assessment using four advanced LLMs, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini, and DeepSeek, which demonstrated a statistically significant positive correlation with human evaluations (Pearson r = 0.67, p < 0.01) while revealing model-specific evaluation patterns. Despite exhibiting rating inflation compared to human assessors, LLMs consistently identified the superiority of constrained generation approaches, providing further validation of our central thesis. items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI or GAI) has gained momentum and become almost indispensable in all areas of daily life. Their use is based on Large Language Models (LLM) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Meta AI, Copilot, Perplexity, claude etc., which often give mind-boggling results for searches in a very specific field. The use of GenAI for lesson planning according to a specific pedagogical approach, and even more so in a developing country such as Cameroon, suffers from a lack of contextual precision because of this problem. Many companies around the world are now developing their own more effective models for specific tasks. However, when it comes to Lesson planning in a sub-Saharan context, few concrete initiatives have been undertaken. In this paper, we propose a conceptual framework for the development of contextualized generative AI for lesson plans using the competency-based learning (CBL) approach. Through a study of CBL-based lesson planning for the secondary education system in Cameroon, we show how this framework can help solve the problem of efficient using of GAI by secondary schools teachers for this purpose.

items.title: Copilot or Culprit? How AI Is Changing Open-Source Bug Reporting and Maintenance
items.abstract: AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. However, they devote more effort to AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than to reports of AI-discovered bugs. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.

items.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
items.abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

items.title: Data Cleaning for Research Data Management: A Human-Supervised, LLM-Assisted Approach
items.abstract: Data cleaning is one of the most labour-intensive steps in research, and large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for it, often without checking what they change. This presentation and hands-on session look at when LLMs help with data cleaning, when they silently do harm, and how to tell the difference (through provenance: tracing every change back to the step that made it). We built an agentic pipeline in which an LLM explores a dataset with code, submits cleaning code one step per problem, and gets back a single score. Every change it makes is logged and evaluated in three layers: data (what happened to the data), behaviour (did the model fix real problems, and fix them right) and provenance (can every change be traced, recomputed and undone). We ran it on the Portal rodent dataset with eight systematically injected errors, comparing models and providers. This record contains: Presentation.pdf: the slides, presented at the Research Data Conference (RDC) 2026, Bern, 20 November 2026. Hands-on.zip: the materials to try it yourself on a sample of 400 artworks from the Tate collection, with eight injected errors and an answer key.

items.title: Data guidelines for the UK kidney community
items.abstract: Kidney research increasingly depends on data that are well-designed, well-governed, and reusable, yet much biomedical data remains poorly described, inconsistently standardised, and difficult to integrate across sources. These community-sourced guidelines, developed through the Renal Health Data Science Network, provide UK kidney researchers with practical, consensus-based recommendations for producing, depositing, and reusing research data. The guidelines are organised around four interconnected themes: patient and clinician engagement; equity and population health; data quality, integration and infrastructure; and methodological rigour and transparency. For each theme, we outline core principles, aims, and practical guidance applicable across the research lifecycle, from study design through to dissemination. Particular attention is given to barriers specific to the kidney patient population, including treatment burden, demographic and cultural diversity, and the needs of the “hidden” early chronic kidney disease population managed in primary care. The guidelines also address the responsible use of artificial intelligence and machine learning in kidney data science, and set out expectations for FAIR data practices and standardised reporting. By articulating shared expectations across these domains, the guidelines aim to improve the quality, equity, and reusability of kidney research data, ultimately supporting more robust and inclusive scientific progress and helping to reduce longstanding health inequalities in kidney disease.

items.title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

items.title: Decolonizing smart education: Localized AI and offline-first digital classrooms for sustainable development in Cameroon
items.abstract: The use of imported, cloud-dependent educational technologies in sub-Saharan Africa often exacerbates infrastructure disparities and introduces epistemological biases through Western-centric artificial intelligence models. This article presents a feasibility study on the implementation of a sovereign EdTech model through the deployment of YAKILI, a localized, locally developed operating system, in Cameroon. Operating offline, the platform incorporates bilingual interactive instruction with the "YAKILI TEACHER BUDDY," an AI assistant designed through fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on the open-source multilingual BLOOM model, in accordance with national curriculum guidelines. Based on an evaluation of a targeted pilot project involving 10 schools, 40 digitized classrooms, 590 teachers, and 7,800 active learners, this study focuses on infrastructure resilience and technical architecture rather than on direct cognitive learning outcomes. Telemetry data reveal a localized network availability rate of 99.8% despite severe disruptions to the external power grid. The results demonstrate that a decentralized AI architecture that prioritizes offline operation can successfully circumvent bottlenecks related to commercial connectivity. The article details mechanisms for mitigating system biases, acknowledges the methodological limitations of the pilot project's designed, particularly the absence of a control group, and provides a transparent framework for the decolonization of smart educational ecosystems in resource-constrained environments.

items.title: Deep learning reveals relationships between muscle and adipose tissue and their associations with age, body mass index, and low back pain: A cross-sectional study in 10,835 subjects
items.abstract: Existing clinical imaging datasets and recent innovations in automated data analysis present a unique opportunity to analyze population-level body composition. We used a large computed tomography (CT) dataset to provide construct validity for artificial intelligence-based opportunistic assessments of body composition, report normative body composition trends, and investigate body composition differences between low back pain and matched control populations at a significantly greater scale than previous work. We applied a deep-learning model to opportunistically compute skeletal muscle, visceral adipose tissue, and subcutaneous adipose tissue cross-sectional areas (CSA) in 23,508 subjects who underwent routine clinical abdominal CT scans and analyzed body composition trends with age and body mass index (BMI). We identified a low back pain cohort using patient electronic health records and created an age-, sex-, and BMI-matched control cohort. We tested for differences in muscle CSA, ratio of visceral to subcutaneous adipose tissue (VAT/SAT), and ratio of muscle to total abdominal adipose tissue (Muscle/TAT). We identified 10,835 (n = 6,121 female) subjects for normative body composition analysis, 2,622 (n = 1,623 female) subjects with low back pain diagnosis, and 2,577 (n = 1,594 female) matched controls. Our population reproduced established rates (5–10% per decade) of muscle loss with age and increasing VAT/SAT ratio in older adults. Our low back pain cohort, 25 times larger than most prior imaging-based low back pain studies, had significantly lower (p < 0.0001) Muscle/TAT ratios than matched controls, albeit with a low effect size (η 2 = 0.004). The low back pain and control groups did not differ in height-squared normalized muscle CSA or VAT/SAT ratio. We showed multiple body composition relationships that matched accepted trends, demonstrating the validity of opportunistic analysis of clinical data for large-scale investigations. In the largest low back pain study of its kind, no meaningful average difference in bulk muscle quantity was detected between low back pain and control populations.

items.title: DeepChem-DEL: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible DEL Modeling and Benchmarking
items.abstract: DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) allow screening of extremely large chemical spaces by tagging compounds with DNA barcodes. Machine learning (ML) techniques have enabled the extraction of meaningful chemical patterns from noisy, target-specific DEL binding data. However, existing tools for DEL machine learning (DEL-ML) remain fragmented, which limits systematic construction and reproducibility of modeling pipelines. Moreover, this fragmentation hinders integration of new models, such as chemical foundation models, into DEL workflows alongside classical approaches. To address these challenges in DEL modeling, we introduce DeepChem-DEL, an open-source suite of reproducible ML workflows for DEL modeling built on the DeepChem ecosystem. DeepChem-DEL integrates (i) a configurable denoising pipeline with (ii) modular DeepChem workflows for enrichment prediction, hit identification, and benchmarking across diverse model classes, including chemical foundation models enabled through extensions to the open-source ChemBERTa-3 framework. We evaluate DeepChem-DEL on the KinDEL and BELKA data sets, reproducing key baselines and enabling direct comparison across model classes. Our experiments demonstrate that leveraging chemical foundation models yields performance competitive with, and in several cases exceeding, previously explored approaches such as graph convolutional networks and random forest models. Together, these results demonstrate that DeepChem-DEL is a scalable and extensible platform for DEL-ML, while highlighting the potential of chemical foundation models for improved DEL modeling and prioritization.

items.title: Deepfake Image Detection Using Transfer Learning Techniques
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of deep learning and generative artificial intelligence has enabled the creation of highly realistic artificial images and videos, commonly known as deepfakes. These manipulated media pose significant challenges to digital security, identity verification, privacy, and information authenticity. Consequently, developing reliable techniques for detecting deepfake content has become an important research challenge. This study proposes a deep learning-based approach for detecting manipulated facial images using transfer learning with the MobileNetV2 architecture. The experimental dataset consists of 1,081 real facial images and 960 fake facial images, with the latter obtained through frame extraction from videos available in the FaceForensics++ dataset. The pre-trained MobileNetV2 model is adapted for binary classification by incorporating global average pooling, a fully connected dense layer, dropout regularization, and a sigmoid output layer. The model is trained to classify facial images into two categories: real and fake. Its performance is evaluated using standard classification metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, and Precision-Recall curve. The experimental findings demonstrate the potential of transfer learning for identifying manipulated facial images using a lightweight convolutional neural network architecture. The study highlights the applicability of MobileNetV2 for deepfake image classification under limited-data conditions and identifies dataset diversity and generalization across different sources as important considerations for further research.

items.title: DeepSkin: A Segmentation-Guided Deep Learning Framework with Generative Augmentation for Dermoscopic Skin Cancer Classification
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has considerable potential to support dermoscopic skin cancer assessment; however, class imbalance, heterogeneous lesion morphology, indistinct lesion boundaries, and imaging variability can limit model generalizability. This study presents DeepSkin, a segmentation-guided deep learning framework integrating lesion segmentation, generative augmentation, and lesion-focused classification. Dermoscopic images were first segmented using a bidirectional ConvLSTM-based U-Net (BCDU-Net), and the resulting lesion regions were used for region-of-interest (ROI) extraction. During classifier development, a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) generated class-conditioned synthetic lesion ROIs to increase training-data diversity and mitigate class imbalance. Real and synthetic training ROIs were subsequently used to train a fine-tuned VGG16 network for binary benign–malignant classification. The framework was developed using the ISIC 2016 dataset, comprising 900 training and 379 test images, and independently evaluated on the PH2 dataset. On ISIC 2016, DeepSkin achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.937 and an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.882 for lesion segmentation, together with a classification accuracy of 96.6% and a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.981. Cross-dataset external evaluation on the independent PH2 dataset, conducted without retraining or fine-tuning, yielded a classification accuracy of 95%. Ablation analysis further demonstrated incremental performance improvements associated with preprocessing, segmentation-guided ROI extraction, and generative augmentation. Grad-CAM visualizations provided qualitative insight into image regions contributing to classification decisions. These findings suggest that integrating generative augmentation with segmentation-guided lesion classification can support accurate dermoscopic image analysis across independent datasets. Further evaluation using larger, diverse, multi-center and prospective clinical datasets is required to establish broader generalizability and clinical applicability.

items.title: Deliberation Within AI: A Reproducible Pipeline for Multi-Agent Deliberation Simulation
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have renewed interest in whether large language models can simulate aspects of public deliberation. Current deliberation simulations remain methodologically fragile: fluent conversational outputs are often treated as evidence of deliberative quality despite limited reproducibility, weak safeguards for viewpoint diversity, and limited systematic evaluation. This article argues that AI-deliberation simulations can function as credible analytical instruments only if they incorporate infrastructures for reproducibility, plurality preservation, and deliberative quality assessment. The article develops a stage-structured method for deliberative simulation combining persona validation, plurality auditing, and discourse-quality assessment within a reproducible pipeline. The framework is presented as a methodological proof-of-concept and evaluated through a simulation study on the June 2023 Swiss federal referendum on the Climate and Innovation Act together with a batch replication study comparing direct and structured deliberation architectures. The findings show that, as an integrated theory-driven architecture, the structured pipeline generates more stable deliberative dynamics than unconstrained interaction, including clearer plurality preservation and more coherent opinion updating. At the same time, the simulations remain below human minipublics in terms of contextual grounding and justificatory depth. The article positions AI-deliberation simulations as methodological infrastructures for cumulative and empirically testable research on AI-supported deliberation in digital governance.

Introduction: PT X Surya Panel has high potential risk of workplace hazards, making the implementation of an Occupational Health and Safety Management System (OHSMS) essential to prevent occupational accidents and protect workers from hazard. An internal OHSMS audit is required to evaluate the extent of OHSMS implementation at PT X Surya Panel Semarang. Method: this study employed a quantitative descriptive evaluative approach conducted in 2024. The sample consisted of 20 employees was selected using purposive sampling. The research variable was the internal OHSMS audit assessment. Data collected through observation, interviews, and document review using a checklist based on 64 criteria stipulated in Government Regulation of the Republic of Indonesia No. 50 of 2012 concerning the Implementation of Occupational Health and Safety Management Systems. Results: The overall internal OHSMS audit achievement score was 76.56%, which categorized as good. However, 7 major nonconformities and 8 minor nonconformities identified. Improvements needed, particularly in the establishment of the Occupational Health and Safety Committee, incident reporting and monitoring systems, to improve the effectiveness and sustainability of OHSMS implementation. Conclusion: The overall implementation of the OSHMS at PT X Surya Panel Semarang categorized as good based on the internal audit assessment, with an achievement score of 76.56%. Nevertheless, priority improvements are required in OHSMS policies, the establishment and functioning of P2K3, incident reporting, and management review.

items.title: Design and Evaluation of Epira: An Automated Interview System for Case Investigation and Contact Tracing
items.abstract: Objective: Case investigation and contact tracing are labor-intensive. Web forms struggle when respondents need clarification before disclosing contacts, and open-ended chatbots may deviate from protocols. We developed and evaluated Epira, a protocol-controlled large language model (LLM) interviewer for multi-disease case investigation and contact tracing. Materials and Methods: Epira pairs LLM dialogue with a rule-based controller enforcing required questions, safety handoffs, and a structured case record, and adapts to new diseases by questionnaire upload. Local (Qwen2.5) and cloud (GPT-5.4) backends were tested. Study 1 used 108 simulated cases with ground-truth fields and contacts for measles and gonorrhea under Epira and open-ended conditions (864 sessions). Study 2 enrolled 72 volunteers in a 2$\times$2 disease-by-model interview assessing completion, usability, acceptability, and trust. Results: Across Study 1, Epira with a local LLM captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts. Open-ended interviewers recovered 31.1-41.9 percentage points fewer required fields than the same models in Epira. In Study 2, completion was 100%; mean adapted System Usability Scale (SUS) was 82.95 $\pm$ 16.17 on a 0-100 scale and mean trust was 3.85 $\pm$ 0.77 on a 1-5 scale. Discussion: Protocol control drove completeness more than model choice. Local and cloud deployments produced similar records, supporting privacy-preserving local use with human review of routed interviews and missed contacts. Conclusion: Epira recovers required fields and contacts under diverse disclosure conditions, works with local and cloud LLMs, and received favorable usability and trust ratings.

items.title: Detection of AI-Generated and Deceptive Fake Reviews on E-Commerce Platforms Using Lightweight Machine Learning
items.abstract: Product reviews shape what people buy, yet their credibility is under a fresh threat: large language models (LLMs) can now mass-produce reviews that are fluent, varied and grammatically flawless. Current detectors cope with this only in part. The best-performing published systems lean on transformer models, paid LLM interfaces or reviewer metadata, resources that smaller platforms often lack, whereas lighter classical models were largely designed around older, human-written spam. We compare five recent studies of fake-review detection, looking at their data, labelling, methods, reported accuracy and acknowledged limitations. Two patterns emerge: accuracy tends to rise together with computational cost, and some of the highest accuracies rest on heuristic or weakly supervised labels, which casts doubt on what they actually measure. Drawing on these observations, we propose a lightweight, interpretable pipeline that pairs TF-IDF n gram features with stylometric indicators of machine generated text and compares four classifiers: Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine and Random Forest. The accompanying evaluation protocol is fully specified and includes stratified hold-out and cross validation, cross-generator and cross-domain tests, paraphrase robustness and ablation. Experimental results for the proposed pipeline are not included in this version, and no performance figures are claimed for it. The system is intended as a risk-scoring aid for human moderators, never as proof of AI authorship.

items.title: Developing and validating the Chinese version of the Perceived Trustworthiness of Large Language Models Scale (PT-LLM-8)
items.abstract: The trustworthiness of technology constitutes a critical determinant of user adoption, particularly regarding artificial intelligence (AI) in daily life. Currently, prominent AI products rely on large language models (LLMs), and such LLMs assist users in personal and professional contexts. To systematically investigate the perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, we provide a psychometrically sound measurement instrument for assessing perceived trustworthiness of LLMs. Given the importance of the Chinese market for current AI developments, the present study examined the psychometric properties of a Chinese version of the Perceived Trustworthiness of Large Language Models Scale (PT-LLM-8) [1] and its association with Big Five personality traits, self-efficacy, and self-esteem. Based on the responses of 478 Chinese adults, the Chinese PT-LLM-8 showed good psychometric properties, including strong internal consistency and a clear unidimensional factor structure. Evidence of construct validity was provided by theoretically expected associations between PT-LLM-8 score and self-efficacy, self-esteem, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness. These findings provide psychometric support for the Chinese version of the PT-LLM-8 as a measure of perceived trustworthiness of LLMs, consistent with the cumulative cross-linguistic evidence for the instrument across its English [1], German [2] and Chinese versions.

items.title: Development and educational evaluation of iLN, a DeepSeek-based generative AI platform for teaching lupus nephritis: a randomized controlled, single-blind (outcome assessor-blinded) study
items.abstract: Lupus nephritis (LN) is the most common and severe organ manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus, and its diagnosis and treatment require the integration of clinical, serological, and renal pathological information. Few studies have evaluated generative artificial intelligence (GAI)-assisted teaching dedicated to LN training. We developed an interactive LN teaching platform (iLN) based on the DeepSeek large language model, integrating current textbooks, guidelines, a renal pathology atlas, and authentic cases across seven modules. In a randomized controlled study, 50 third-year medical students were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to iLN-based multimodal teaching (iLN group) or traditional lectures (control group). Randomization was performed using a random number table after all participants had been enrolled, and the outcome assessor was blinded to group allocation. The primary outcome was an immediate postintervention 20-item multiple-choice examination (100 points). The iLN group achieved a higher median score compared to the control group (median 90 [IQR 90–95] vs. 75 [IQR 75–80]; Hodges–Lehmann median difference of 15.0 points, 95% CI 10.0–20.0; Mann–Whitney U test P < 0.001). There was no significant difference in score dispersion between the groups, as the 95% confidence interval for the ratio of standard deviations included 1.0. The nominally smaller standard deviation does not provide evidence that the platform reduced variation in learning outcomes. Additionally, iLN students reported a high satisfaction rate of 96.0%. The iLN platform was associated with higher immediate post-intervention test scores and high student satisfaction, supporting the feasibility of integrating generative AI into a multicomponent platform for LN. Larger multicenter studies with validated instruments and long-term follow-up are required. NCT07706998 (retrospectively registered on June 30, 2026).

items.title: Development of a Virtual Reality Learning Environment for Computer Assembly Competency in Pre-Service Teachers Using Generative AI-Produced Media
items.abstract: Thai computer teacher trainees must assemble and repair computers during their practicum, yet many get little hands-on practice because laboratory machines are scarce, outdated, and easily damaged. This design-and-development study built a virtual reality learning environment (VRLE) for computer assembly on a Meta Quest 3 headset, with controller-free hand tracking, three simulation rooms mapped to a national occupational competency unit, and learning media produced with generative AI. Development followed the ADDIE model, and a feasibility tryout used a one-group pretest–posttest design. Three content experts and three technical experts rated content (M = 4.74) and technical quality (M = 4.45) as very good, with interaction and usability the weakest domain (M = 4.11). Among 35 pre-service teachers with matched tests, achievement rose from 8.20 to 9.09 out of 10 (Wilcoxon z = 2.95, p = .002, r = .50; t(34) = 2.92, dz = 0.49). After a sequence of website lessons, VR practice, real-hardware practice, and debriefing, mean competency on real hardware was 4.85 (n = 36) and mean satisfaction was 4.79 (n = 28), both with ceiling effects. Without a control group, the results show that the VRLE is feasible and well received, not that it caused the gains.

items.title: Development of research competence of undergraduates through training in text linguistics based on artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Introduction This study addresses the development of undergraduates' research competence through teaching Text Linguistics by integrating artificial intelligence tools. The study aims to develop a scientific and methodological model and experimentally evaluate its effectiveness. Methods A mixed-methods quasi-experimental design was employed involving 58 first-year undergraduates enrolled in the Kazakh Language and Literature educational program. The experimental group consisted of 30 students, while the control group included 28 students. ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity AI, Elicit, Consensus, and Scite.ai were integrated into tasks involving scientific text analysis, academic writing, literature review, evaluation of scientific evidence, and research reflection. Research competence was assessed using a 100-point test, scientific text analysis tasks, a Likert-scale questionnaire, and an expert assessment rubric. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, the Shapiro-Wilk test, paired and independent t-tests, Cohen's d, and Cronbach's alpha. Results The experimental group's research competence score increased from 58.43 ± 6.87 to 84.27 ± 5.94 points. The improvement was statistically significant ( p < 0.001), with a large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.92). Discussion The findings indicate that the systematic pedagogical integration of artificial intelligence tools into Text Linguistics instruction can support the development of undergraduates' scientific text analysis, academic writing, critical thinking, evidence-based reasoning, and research independence.

items.title: Didactic orchestration integrating artificial intelligence tools to develop creative thinking skills in students
items.abstract: Introduction This study examined changes in students' self-reported creativity-related behaviors following an educational intervention combining artificial intelligence (AI) tools and the DRAE instructional model (Diagnosis, Recreation, Application, and Estimation). Methods A one-group preexperimental pretest-posttest questionnaire design was complemented by semi-structured interviews and direct-observation records. The quantitative analysis included 551 valid paired EvaCreIA records, exceeding the minimum sample target of 543. The questionnaire assessed Generate Diverse Ideas (GID), Generate Creative Ideas (GIC), and Evaluate and Improve Ideas (EMI). Complementary interview indicators were calculated from 703 eligible pretest and 730 eligible posttest records, while direct observation included 568 completed checklist records. Results Posttest means exceeded pretest means by 0.222, 0.270, and 0.241 points for GID, GIC, and EMI, respectively, on a five-point scale. Wilcoxon signed-rank comparisons remained statistically significant after Holm adjustment ( p < .001). Rank-biserial correlations were 0.340 for GID, 0.387 for GIC, 0.340 for EMI, and 0.374 for the supplementary overall score. The complementary interview indicators showed higher favorable-response percentages at posttest. Discussion The results indicate changes in self-reported creativity-related behaviors following the combined educational intervention. However, retrospective record linkage, limitations in cross-instrument correspondence, self-report measurement, and the absence of a comparison group restrict causal interpretation. The findings do not establish an independent causal effect of AI or validate the DRAE model.

items.title: Digital Agriculture and Plant Genomics for Predictive Breeding
items.abstract: Digital sensing, genomic prediction and increasingly accessible computational methods are changing how crop breeders observe environments, characterise genetic variation and prioritise candidate varieties. Yet the central question is not whether more data improve predictive fit, but whether combining information sources produces reliable, timely and economically worthwhile selection decisions outside the circumstances in which models were trained. This critical narrative review examines the convergence of plant genomics, field phenomics, environmental characterisation and artificial intelligence in predictive breeding. Peer-reviewed research and methodological literature published from 2001 to 11 September 2026 were critically selected through accessible scholarly sources and citation tracing, with attention to empirical comparisons, validation design and translational relevance. Genomic prediction provides a well-established foundation, whereas phenomic and environmental covariates yield more conditional benefits. Contrasting wheat studies illustrate that spectral and thermal information can improve prediction in some settings but can also introduce noise or fail under forward validation. Environmental descriptors become more informative when aligned with developmental stage and the target population of environments; flexible machine-learning architectures do not consistently outperform appropriately specified statistical baselines. Structural variation, pangenomes, multi-omics and genomic language models broaden the biological information available to breeders, although evidence of additional realised genetic gain remains limited for several emerging approaches. Major weaknesses include information leakage, unrepresentative validation partitions, incompatible field metadata, uncertainty neglected during selection, and scarce evaluation of operational costs and varietal delivery. The review develops a decision-centred framework in which data collection, model complexity and evaluation are governed by the breeding decision and the information genuinely available at that point. The strongest near-term opportunities lie in prospective multi-environment validation, careful phenomic measurement, stage-aware environmental modelling and interoperable datasets. Predictive breeding is therefore best understood as a disciplined integration of biological understanding, field experimentation and statistical evidence, not as a replacement for them.

items.title: Digital technologies in construction material manufacturing: A systematic review of applications, performance outcomes, and integration frameworks
items.abstract: The construction sector consumes roughly 36 percent of global energy and generates 40 percent of carbon dioxide emissions, which makes the way building materials are produced a pressing sustainability problem. This paper reviews, systematically, how digital technologies are applied in construction material manufacturing. The review pursues three aims: to identify the main technology domains, to assess what they deliver in practice, and to propose a conceptual framework for their integration. Searches of Scopus and Web of Science returned 112 peer-reviewed studies, which were analysed thematically and mapped bibliometrically. Five principal domains emerged: artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) for quality prediction; Internet of Things (IoT) process monitoring; additive manufacturing (AM); digital twin (DT) simulation; and Building Information Modeling (BIM) combined with lifecycle assessment (LCA). The evidence points in one direction. Product quality, operational efficiency and environmental performance all improve, with material waste falling by 30–60 percent, prediction errors by 18–17 percent, and procurement lead times by 27 percent on average. Combination matters more than any single tool: gains grew substantially when technologies were used together rather than alone, so integrated adoption outperforms a piecemeal one. The proposed framework offers practical direction for manufacturers, researchers and policymakers working on the digital transformation of construction material production.

items.title: DIGITALIZATION, CIRCULARITY AND GEOPOLITICAL RISKS AS DRIVERS OF GLOBAL FASHION INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENT
items.abstract: The article investigates the transformation of the global fashion industry in the first half of the 2020s under the combined influence of digitalization, circularity and geopolitical risks. Its purpose is to explain how these drivers reshape value creation, the geography of production, market access and the economic security of global value-chain participants. The study applies systemic and structural-functional approaches, comparative analysis, content analysis of regulatory requirements in major importing markets and elements of scenario-based synthesis. A development driver is defined as a persistent factor that, over several business cycles, changes costs and value added, the spatial organization of production and sales, and the institutional conditions of international trade. An integrated analytical framework is proposed that connects the three drivers with four transmission mechanisms: costs, speed, regulatory compliance and demand. Digitalization influences product development, forecasting, supply-chain coordination and traceability; however, artificial intelligence may either limit excess production or accelerate the proliferation of short-lived collections. Circularity creates additional value through resale, repair, rental and material recovery, while requiring reliable product information and reverse logistics. Geopolitical risks, including trade restrictions, logistics disruptions and origin verification, shift sourcing priorities from the lowest purchase price towards supply reliability and compliance. The analysis identifies complementarities between digital identification and circular operations, supply-chain visibility and resilience, and local reuse and reduced dependence on distant manufacturing. Conflicts arise when accelerated assortment renewal undermines circular objectives, nearshoring raises production costs, or new compliance requirements disadvantage smaller suppliers. The resulting configuration of global value chains combines geographically diversified sourcing, verifiable product data, reverse flows and supplier selection based on resilience rather than price alone. Four operational criteria are suggested: the number of genuinely alternative production nodes, the share of products with a verifiable digital record, the ability to reallocate production within a quarter and the availability of circular arrangements in priority markets. For Ukraine, opportunities for nearshore supply to the European Union depend on the capacity to manage wartime disruptions, demonstrate traceability and upgrade beyond cut-make-trim operations towards product development and digital order support. items.title: DiLE: Discrimination-Aware Latent-Space Learning for Universal Multimodal Embeddings
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models have greatly improved input understanding in universal multimodal embedding models. However, this understanding does not ensure that their embeddings preserve the evidence needed to distinguish relevant items from confusable alternatives. To preserve essential discriminative evidence in embeddings, this paper proposes DiLE, a discrimination-aware latent-space learning framework that combines task guidance with on-policy retrieval feedback. Specifically, a few learnable queries are used to encode task-relevant information in a compact latent space. Reasoning instructions and auxiliary answer-generation supervision shape these representations to support both task understanding and retrieval discrimination. To address task-specific discriminative needs, we design shared-private expert adaptation that integrates cross-task knowledge sharing with task-specific representation learning. Building on this, the on-policy hard-negative distillation is introduced: the student retrieves confusable candidates, and a reverse KL divergence objective aligns its embedding-based similarity distribution with the teacher's fine-grained relevance distribution over these candidates. Candidates are periodically refreshed using updated student snapshots, tying teacher supervision to the student's evolving retrieval behavior and confusions. Across four model configurations that span two backbone generations, DiLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v2, UVRB, and MRMR, demonstrating its effectiveness across modalities and tasks.
